title: hardware-comparison-benchmarks-a100-h100-l40s-cloud-skus-cuda-drivers-notes
body:
Objective:
We ran a cross-hardware, cross-driver set of micro- and macro-benchmarks to characterize inference performance and dominant bottlenecks in the serving runtime. Focused targets: A100 (various cloud SKUs), H100 (various cloud SKUs), and NVIDIA L40S. Secondary variables: CUDA toolkit and NVIDIA driver versions, instance type (PCIe/NVLink), and host CPU configuration.

Summary (high level):
- H100 consistently gives the best tokens/sec for large models (70B+), ~2.5-3x vs A100 on the same cloud SKU when using CUDA 12.x + recent drivers.
- L40S sits between A100 and H100 for most workloads; it is cost-efficient for medium models (7B-13B) but underperforms H100 for large-model sharded inference.
- Driver/CUDA combo matters: H100 saw a ~15-25% regression on older driver/CUDA stacks (eg driver 510 + CUDA 11.7) vs driver 535 + CUDA 12.1. A100 is more forgiving but still benefits from newer kernels.
- Bottlenecks observed: kernel launch/attention kernel selection on >32k sequence lengths, PCIe host-to-device bandwidth for multi-host NVLink-less setups, and host CPU overhead during batching/IO for tiny batch sizes.

Test harness & methodology:
- Harness: internal bench runner (bench/run_bench.py) capturing per-step timing, GPU util, GPU memory, host CPU, NVLink counters where available, and detailed kernel timelines using Nsight Systems sampling.
- Models: Llama2-7B (fp16), Llama2-13B (fp16), Llama2-70B (bf16/fp16 where supported).
- Workloads: single-stream generation (batch=1, generate=512 tokens), small-batch throughput (batch=8, generate=256), and multi-stream concurrency (8 concurrent single-streams).
- Measurement: warmup 20 iterations, then 200 measured iterations. Reported: median tokens/sec, p95 latency per step, and 95th-percentile memory.
- Environment controls: pinned CPU governor, isolated NUMA node where possible, RMM/allocator set to static pool to avoid host-side malloc noise.

Configurations tested (representative samples):
- A100 (a100-80gb-v2, PCIe vs NVLink), driver 525/CUDA 11.8, driver 535/CUDA 12.1
- H100 (h100-80gb, NVLink enabled on HBM clusters), driver 535/CUDA 12.1, driver 545/CUDA 12.2 (early tests)
- L40S (l40s-48gb sku), driver 535/CUDA 12.1
- Host types: c6gn/c7gn-style for A100 where available, and CPU-rich M-series for H100 tests.

Representative results (median tokens/sec, single-stream, generate=512):
- Llama2-7B (fp16): A100 (a100-80gb) = 480 tok/s; L40S = 720 tok/s; H100 = 980 tok/s.
- Llama2-13B (fp16): A100 = 220 tok/s; L40S = 340 tok/s; H100 = 740 tok/s.
- Llama2-70B (bf16): A100 = 60 tok/s; L40S = 110 tok/s; H100 = 170 tok/s.
Notes: numbers are medians across 3 runs, variance +-5% under identical infra. Absolute numbers will vary by model implementation and attention kernel choices; these are representative to highlight ratios.

Latency (p95) single-token generation, 70B (micro):
- A100 p95 = 120 ms
- L40S p95 = 90 ms
- H100 p95 = 55 ms

Driver / CUDA sensitivity:
- H100 on driver 510 + CUDA 11.7 showed a throughput regression (~15-25%) vs driver 535 + CUDA 12.1 for 70B workloads. Root cause: missing optimized attention/softmax kernel paths in the older CUDA/cuBLAS/cuDNN stack; Nsight traces show extra fallback kernels called.
- A100 saw smaller differences (~5-10%) but stability improved on driver 535.
- Recommendation: standardize on driver 535 + CUDA 12.1 across clusters for now; re-test when 12.2/545 driver is declared stable by NVIDIA and cloud vendors.

Profiling observations & bottlenecks:
1) Kernel selection & fused kernels:
- H100 benefited from newer fused attention kernels and tensor-core paths that drastically reduced overall kernel count per token. Nsight timelines show 30-40% fewer kernel launches for H100 runs when using CUDA 12.x stacks.

2) PCIe host-device transfer pressure (multi-input batch assembly):
- In multi-tenant / multi-request scenarios where prefix caching is disabled and many small requests are assembled on the host, observed host-to-device copies (and CPU memcpy) saturating PCIe on older instance families. This increases tail latency for small-batch workloads.
- Mitigation: enable prefix/KV caching, use pinned pages and batched H2D transfers, and prefer instance types with NVLink for high concurrency.

3) NVLink / inter-GPU comm for model parallelism:
- For model-sharded 70B across 8 GPUs, NVLink presence reduced all-reduce times significantly; A100 NVLink bridges yielded ~20% better throughput vs PCIe-only multi-GPU on the same SKU. H100 NVLink topology + newer drivers gave the best multi-GPU efficiency.

4) Host CPU overhead & python boundary costs:
- For tiny batch sizes (1-2), Python-level tensor prep and scheduler locks contributed 10-25% of per-token time. We measured this by comparing a C++-driven runner vs python runner. C++ runner cut p50 latency by ~15% for 7B.
- Recommendation: critical production paths should use the compiled runner / minimal Python trampoline.

5) GPU memory fragmentation / allocator behavior:
- Observed occasional OOM-like slowdowns when the allocator attempted device-side allocations mid-run under certain dynamic batch patterns. Using a large static arena allocator reduced variance and removed intermittent spikes.

Cloud SKU notes (observed differences between cloud SKUs for the same GPU):
- Instance type matters: same GPU SKU but different machine families (e.g., cpu type, PCIe lanes available, and memory bandwidth to the host) caused a 5-15% spread. Avoid mixing instance types in the same auto-scaling pool for tight SLOs.
- Some cloud SKUs ship with slightly different driver/kernel combinations by default; always reimage or validate drivers to the standardized stack.

Operational recommendations (short):
- Default stack: NVIDIA driver 535 + CUDA 12.1 for all new clusters; test 545/12.2 in staging.
- Use H100 for latency-sensitive, large-model production; A100 is still cost-effective for mid-sized models and workloads tolerant to slightly higher tail latency. L40S is a strong mid-market option for many 13B workloads.
- Enforce static device memory pool allocator in production images to avoid runtime fragmentation spikes.
- For high concurrency small requests, prefer NVLink-enabled instances or aggressively use prefix/KV caching and batching.
- Move hot execution path to compiled runner to avoid Python scheduling overhead for p95 important endpoints.

Next steps / action items:
- [Priya] Run a 545/12.2 validation matrix across critical SKUs and report deltas by 2026-03-05.
- [Jordan] Re-run multi-host PCIe-only 70B tests with detailed Nsight traces to isolate remaining all-reduce overheads by 2026-02-28.
- [SRE] Standardize golden AMI with driver 535 + CUDA 12.1 and static allocator; roll to a single test pool for consistent benching.
- Add automated nightly bench jobs that vary CUDA/driver permutations and upload metrics to the benchmark dashboard.

Appendix A - Example commands (used to produce the numbers above):
- python bench/run_bench.py --model l2-7b --dtype fp16 --batch 1 --generate 512 --warmup 20 --iter 200 --cuda 12.1 --driver 535 --allocator arena
- python bench/run_bench.py --model l2-70b --dtype bf16 --shard multi --gpus 8 --generate 512 --cuda 12.1 --driver 535
- nsight-sys --trace=cuda,nvtx --output=trace_h100_70b.qdrep python bench/run_bench.py ...

Appendix B - Quick checklist for repeatable runs:
- Reimage to golden AMI (driver 535 + CUDA 12.1).
- Ensure NUMA pinning and CPU isolation (taskset/cgroup) for consistency.
- Disable power-saving governor on CPU and enable persistence mode on GPU.
- Use same docker image + pinned pip wheel versions (list in linked GH PR).

Notes to reviewers: numbers are preliminary and reflect our current runtime kernel selection paths. We want feedback on additional cloud SKUs to include (I tested the most common ones we use in production) and whether to expand the matrix to include older CUDA 11.x stacks for customers who cannot upgrade yet.

-- Alex
